newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: Austria telecoms offer untapped potential - analysts.
newsitem.headline: Austria telecoms offer untapped potential - analysts.

text.p: One of Austria's last bastions of state-run industry, post and telecoms monopoly PTA, is a source of vast potential yet to be exploited and doubly attractive after a link-up with Italy's Stet, say analysts.

"Austria is among the remaining few European post and telecom companies that have not yet come to the market and all of these have enormous untapped potential," said Evan Miller, analyst at CSFB in London.

Post und Telekom Austria AG (PTA), which consists of the state postal service, Austria's only terrestrial telephone network and the largest bus service in the country, must by law be privatised in 1999.

The company on Wednesday announced that it had sold a 25 percent stake in Mobilkom, its mobile phone unit, to Italy's Stet for 8.4 billion schillings ($695 million) -- a sum which surprised even PTA and which some analysts said was too much.

Stet managing director Tomaso Tommasi di Vignano said in a statement released in Rome that the company expected mobile phones to account for a quarter of the Austrian telephone market by the year 2000, up from 8.75 percent currently.

"Austria has been one of the least liberalised markets in Europe till now and this is a definite step towards liberalisation becoming more established," Jim Ross, analyst at ABN Amro Hoare Govett, said of the deal.
"This leads on to competition in the fixed telephony side of things later. I would think the organisations that lost will wonder if they should start getting into that," he added.

Stet had been competing against rival offers from Tele Danmark, the Unicom unit of the international Unisource alliance and U.S. group South Western Bell, whose offers were reported to have been substantially below Stet's.

Mobilkom operates Austria's biggest global system for mobile communications (GSM) network with some 400,000 customers. Its chief rival is max.mobil, which is owned by a private consortium and has around 20,000 subscribers.

The Austrian government plans to award a third mobile phone licence in June to boost competition ahead of the planned liberalisation of the Austrian telecommunications sector in 1998 in line with European Union regulations.
Wolfgang Fingernagel, spokesman for the ministry of science and transport which deals with telecoms, voiced concern that Austrian companies could be dwarfed by giant conglomerates.

"It won't be very easy for Austrian companies, which are small players on the international market, to survive if they try alone and if they team up with bigger foreign companies they risk losing their independence," he said.
Loss-making PTA, which has a workforce of 55,000, aims to turn into a profitable, competitive company by 1998 without stinging job cuts or demerging.
In any case, most of PTA's staff are civil servants and protected from redundancy by Austrian law.
PTA finance chief Johannes Ditz insists the company's three divisions will all be in the black by 1999.

The former economics minister plans to achieve a pre-tax profit of 13 billion schillings by 1998 -- a tall order given that the bus service made a 500 million schilling loss in 1996 and the postal business a loss of one billion schillings.

"It's wrong to be too pessimistic," said CSFB's Miller. "We might not have thought possible what some of their peers have already achieved in terms of very necessary structural changes and downsizing.
"Paradoxically the companies that have less efficient starting points in many cases have proven the most attractive investments because there is viewed to be huge upside potential," he noted.
Past success stories in privatisation include Dutch telecoms utility KNP, British Telecom and Deutsche Telekom, which was five times oversubscribed.

The first of PTA's reforms will be the introduction of new telephone tariffs in November. Peak-time prices will be raised while calls made after business hours will be cheaper. Internet rates will also be drastically reduced.
The postal service is due for a major overhaul and will in future offer an express package delivery service as well as financial services. ($ = 12.08 Austrian Schillings)
